claim: Roughly 50,000 quantifiable macroscopic plant parts were retrieved from fine-sifted flotation and dry-sieved sediment samples of the middens of Elusa, Shivta, and Nessana.
source: Roughly 50,000 quantifiable macroscopic plant parts were retrieved from fine-sifted flotation and dry-sieved sediment samples of the middens of Elusa, Shivta, and Nessana, excluding charcoal and in addition to a roughly equal number retrieved from wet-sieving.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific count of plant parts retrieved from the excavation sites.

claim: The plant remains were identified to a total of 144 distinct plant taxa.
source: These mostly seed and fruit (carpological) remains were identified to a total of 144 distinct plant taxa (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of distinct taxa identified from the samples.

claim: Nearly half of the identified specimens were derived from six Shivta middens.
source: Nearly half of the identified specimens were derived from six Shivta middens, one quarter from three Elusa middens, and one quarter from two Nessana middens.
evidence: The manuscript provides the distribution of specimens across the three sites.

claim: The Early Islamic middens from Shivta and Nessana displayed a higher diversity of finds.
source: Preservation quality varied somewhat within and between middens and samples, the richest of which were the Early Islamic middens from Shivta and Nessana, which also displayed a higher diversity of finds (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript states that Early Islamic middens had higher diversity based on the data.

claim: Twenty-three domesticated food plant taxa were identified by carpological remains.
source: Twenty-three domesticated food plant taxa were identified by carpological remains, including cereals, legumes, fruits, nuts, and one vegetable.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of domesticated food plant taxa identified.

claim: Barley, wheat, and grape were the main cultivated crops based on seed quantities and ubiquity.
source: Seed quantities and ubiquity point to barley (Hordeum vulgare L.), wheat (Triticum turgidum/aestivum), and grape (Vitis vinifera L.) as the main cultivated crops, which were clearly calorific staples.
evidence: The manuscript identifies these crops as main staples based on quantitative data.

claim: Local cultivation of barley, wheat, and grape is attested to by cereal processing waste and wine-pressing waste.
source: Their local cultivation is attested to by cereal processing waste (rachis fragments, awn and glume fragments, culm nodes, and rhizomes) and wine-pressing waste (grape pips, skins, and pedicels).
evidence: The manuscript provides evidence of local cultivation through processing waste.

claim: Lentils, bitter vetch, fig, date, and olive should be counted as staples based on seed quantities and ubiquity.
source: In addition, lentils (Lens culinaris Medik. syn. Vicia lens [L.] Coss. & Germ.), bitter vetch (Vicia ervilia [L.] Willd.), fig (Ficus carica L.), date (Phoenix dactylifera L.), and olive (Olea europaea L.) should also be counted as staples based on seed quantities and ubiquity (Table 4; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript identifies these as staples based on quantitative data.

claim: All identified staples were among the Southwest Asian Neolithic founder crops and early fruit domesticates.
source: Significantly, all identified staples were among the Southwest Asian Neolithic founder crops and early fruit domesticates which formed a stable part of Levantine diets by the end of the Chalcolithic (c. 4500–3300 BCE).
evidence: The manuscript categorizes the staples based on established knowledge of Neolithic crops.

claim: Grapes were the primary cash crop of the Byzantine Negev Highlands, particularly in the mid-5th to mid-6th c. CE.
source: Grapes were previously shown to be the primary cash crop of the Byzantine Negev Highlands, particularly in the mid-5th to mid-6th c. CE, based on their changing relative frequencies (Fuks et al., 2020b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that demonstrated this finding.

claim: Free-threshing hexaploid bread wheat appears in the Negev Highlands only after the mid-6th c.
source: Interestingly, free-threshing hexaploid bread wheat (Triticum aestivum s.l.)—a more market-oriented wheat species identifiable archaeologically by indicative rachis segments—appears in the Negev Highlands only after the mid-6th c. (Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal appearance of this wheat species based on data in Table 4.

claim: The appearance of bread wheat corresponds with the period of decline in viticulture.
source: This corresponds with the period of decline in viticulture (Fuks et al., 2020b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing the decline in viticulture.

claim: Aubergine seeds from Shivta are among the earliest archaeobotanical finds of this plant in the Levant.
source: Together with seeds from Abbasid Jerusalem, seeds from the Negev Highland middens are among the earliest archaeobotanical finds of this plant in the Levant and are roughly contemporaneous with the earliest textual references to aubergine in the region (Watson, 1983; Amar, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript compares the finds with other early records and textual references.

claim: The sediment sample from Shivta containing aubergine seeds was dated to the Abbasid period (772–974 cal CE at 2σ).
source: The sediment sample from Shivta containing aubergine seeds was dated to the Abbasid period (772–974 cal CE at 2σ), supporting previous finds from Abbasid Jerusalem (Amichay et al., 2019; Amichay and Weiss, 2020; Samuel, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript provides radiocarbon dating results for the sample.

claim: Aubergine is the only summer crop in the Negev Highlands plant assemblage.
source: Significantly, aubergine is the only summer crop in the Negev Highlands plant assemblage.
evidence: The manuscript identifies aubergine as unique among the crops found.

claim: RAD and IGR crops make up over a third of the domesticated species found in the Negev Highland middens.
source: While their quantities and ubiquities indicate that RAD and IGR crops were initially of minor significance, they make up over a third of the domesticated species found in the Negev Highland middens (Figure 4, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative analysis and refers to Figure 4 for visualization.

claim: Only aubergine among the Negev Highland plant remains is an IGR crop.
source: Of the Negev Highland plant remains, only aubergine is an IGR crop (Figures 4–5; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and refers to figures for support.

claim: Roughly one-third of the domesticated food plants found in the Negev Highlands were introduced to the Southern Levant between the 1st c. BCE and the 4th c. CE.
source: By contrast, the Negev Highlands crop basket highlights the influence of RAD, particularly on arboriculture. Roughly one-third of the domesticated food plants found in the Negev Highlands were evidently introduced to the Southern Levant between the 1st c. BCE and the 4th c. CE.
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative assessment of RAD crop introductions.

claim: RAD crops identified by carpological remains include pistachio, stone pine, peach, plum/cherry, jujube, and white lupine.
source: Among those identified by carpological remains are pistachio, stone pine, peach, plum/cherry, jujube, and white lupine, plus carob which is a local wild species but was apparently not fully domesticated until the Hellenistic-Roman period (Van der Veen and Hamilton-Dyer, 1998; Vermeeren and Cappers, 2002; Bouby and Marinval, 2004; Bosi et al., 2020; Figure 4; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript lists RAD crops and cites supporting literature.

claim: Hazel is an additional RAD species identified in the Negev Highlands by pollen remains.
source: Considering pollen remains, hazel is an additional RAD species identified in the Negev Highlands by pollen remains; its pollen was also found in Herod's garden at Caesarea, probably as an imported ornamental (Langgut, 2022), and endocarp remains were retrieved from the Nahal Arugot cave inhabited by Bar Kokhba rebels in 135 CE (Kislev and Simchoni, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript identifies hazel from pollen data and cites comparative finds.

claim: Nile acacia is considered a RAD crop introduced from Egypt.
source: Although not a food plant, we also consider Nile acacia to be a RAD crop introduced from Egypt, as noted above.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the Nile acacia finds as evidence of introduction.

claim: RAD plant remains are more prevalent in the Early Islamic phase likely due to better preservation and plant richness.
source: The fact that the RAD plant remains are more prevalent in the Early Islamic phase (Supplementary file 2) is likely the result of overall better preservation and plant richness in this phase.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the data pattern.

claim: The earliest secure archaeobotanical records of RAD crops in the Southern Levant derive mostly from the 1st c. BCE to the 2nd c. CE.
source: Therefore, we understand them to be part of the general Late Antique Negev Highlands domesticated plant assemblage, noting that their earliest secure archaeobotanical records in the Southern Levant as a whole derive mostly from the 1st c. BCE to the 2nd c. CE (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the temporal distribution of RAD crop records.

claim: RAD was a greater force in the agricultural history of the first millennium CE than the IGR.
source: Altogether, this evidence suggests that RAD was a greater force in the agricultural history of the first millennium CE than the IGR, which is also the current consensus from Iberia (Peña-Chocarro et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion based on the data and cites supporting consensus.

claim: The first millennium CE was an unprecedented period of change for local crop-plant species diversity in the Eastern Mediterranean.
source: Clearly, the first millennium CE was an unprecedented period of change for local crop-plant species diversity in the Eastern Mediterranean and beyond.
evidence: The manuscript makes a broad interpretive claim based on the evidence presented.

claim: Inhabitants of the Levant and Eastern Mediterranean region continued to rely primarily on Neolithic founder crops and early fruit domesticates until the end of the first millennium CE.
source: Yet the evidence presented here demonstrates that even the combined forces underlying first millennium CE crop diffusion affected, but did not immediately transform, people's diets. At least until the end of that millennium, inhabitants of the Levant and Eastern Mediterranean region continued to rely primarily on long-tried and tested Neolithic founder crops and early fruit domesticates.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the data to show continuity in dietary staples.

claim: Plants first attested to in the Southern Levant during the first millennium CE account for one-third of the domesticated plant species diversity in the Late Antique Negev Highland assemblages.
source: This is evident from Late Antique Negev Highland archaeobotanical assemblages within which plants first attested to in the Southern Levant during this period account for one-third of the domesticated plant species diversity—more than any other period represented in the assemblage (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative analysis and refers to Figure 4.

claim: The first millennium CE contributed more to global agricultural diversity than any earlier period.
source: Altogether the evidence supports a gradualist model for Holocene-wide crop diffusion, within which the first millennium CE contributed more to global agricultural diversity than any earlier period.
evidence: The manuscript makes a broad comparative claim based on the data.

claim: Specimen counts and ubiquity of RAD and IGR plant species are very low in the Negev Highland assemblages.
source: However, specimen counts and ubiquity of both RAD and IGR plant species are very low in the Negev Highland assemblages, indicating slow incorporation into local foodways and agriculture.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative data on specimen counts and ubiquity.

claim: The low specimen counts and ubiquity of RAD and IGR crops indicate slow incorporation into local foodways and agriculture.
source: However, specimen counts and ubiquity of both RAD and IGR plant species are very low in the Negev Highland assemblages, indicating slow incorporation into local foodways and agriculture.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the quantitative data to infer adoption patterns.

claim: The Islamic Green Revolution involved a package of sub-/tropical, mostly East- and South Asian domesticates which spread into Mediterranean lands ca. 700–1100 CE according to Andrew Watson.
source: According to Andrew Watson, the IGR involved a package of sub-/tropical, mostly East- and South Asian domesticates which, as a result of Islamicate territorial expansion, spread into Mediterranean lands along with requisite irrigation technologies ca. 700–1100 CE.
evidence: The manuscript cites Watson's thesis about the IGR.

claim: The IGR allegedly involved some 17 domesticated plant taxa according to Watson.
source: This allegedly involved some 17 domesticated plant taxa (Table 1), including such economically significant crops as sugar cane, orange, and banana (Watson, 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites Watson's claim about the number of IGR crops.

claim: Critics have argued that many proposed IGR crops were of minor economic significance or were previously cultivated in the Mediterranean region.
source: However, critics have argued that many of the proposed IGR crops were, and still are, of minor economic significance, while others were previously cultivated in the Mediterranean region, particularly under Roman rule, or else arrived much later (Decker, 2009a; Johns, 1984; Ashtor, 1985).
evidence: The manuscript cites critical perspectives on the IGR thesis.

claim: Several East- and Central Asian crops appear to have been first introduced to the Mediterranean region during the Roman period, 1st c. BCE–4th c. CE.
source: Indeed, there is considerable evidence for crop diffusion immediately preceding and during the Roman period in the Eastern Mediterranean, 1st c. BCE–4th c. CE. During this time, several East- and Central Asian crops, including some of those on Watson's IGR list (e.g. lemon, rice), appear to have been first introduced to the Mediterranean region, along with agricultural technologies (Decker, 2009a; Johns, 1984; Ashtor, 1985; Decker, 2009b; Kamash, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources documenting Roman-period crop introductions.

claim: A growing fruit basket is evident in sites and texts of the Eastern Mediterranean region from the Roman period on.
source: From this period on, a growing fruit basket is evident in sites and texts of the Eastern Mediterranean region (Amar, 2000; Kislev and Simchoni, 2006; Aubaile, 2012; Amichay et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources documenting the expansion of fruit crops.

claim: Several tree fruits such as peach, pear, plum, hazel, and others were introduced during the Roman period.
source: These include several tree fruits such as peach, pear, plum, hazel, and others (Table 2) apparently reflecting the Greco-Roman passion for grafting and its pivotal role in the dispersal of mostly temperate fruit crops from Central Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe (Zohary et al., 2012; Mudge et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript lists tree fruits and cites sources on grafting and dispersal.

claim: Greco-Roman grafting played a pivotal role in the dispersal of temperate fruit crops from Central Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe.
source: These include several tree fruits such as peach, pear, plum, hazel, and others (Table 2) apparently reflecting the Greco-Roman passion for grafting and its pivotal role in the dispersal of mostly temperate fruit crops from Central Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe (Zohary et al., 2012; Mudge et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites sources on the role of grafting in crop dispersal.

claim: Roman arboricultural diffusion is a subset of Roman agricultural diffusion (RAD).
source: Yet Roman arboricultural diffusion is but a subset of Roman agricultural diffusion (hereafter, RAD), which also includes non-arboreal crops (including hemp, muskmelon, white lupine, rice, sorghum) and various agricultural techniques diffused by the Romans into the Eastern Mediterranean (Kamash, 2012; Mercuri et al., 2002; Pelling, 2005; Cappers, 2006; Van der Veen, 2011; Wilson, 2002; Kron, 2012; Avital, 2014; Van der Veen et al., 2008; Butzer et al., 1985).
evidence: The manuscript defines RAD and cites multiple sources documenting it.

claim: Not all crops in motion during the Roman period took hold in local agriculture.
source: Not all crops in motion during this period took hold in local agriculture.
evidence: The manuscript makes a general observation about crop adoption patterns.

claim: Roman-period importation of rice in Egypt was followed by local cultivation in the Islamic period.
source: In some cases, as has been claimed for rice in Egypt, Roman-period importation of the new crops was followed by local cultivation in the Islamic period (Van der Veen et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a source documenting the trajectory of rice cultivation in Egypt.

claim: Some Roman introductions were subsequently abandoned.
source: In other cases, Roman introductions were subsequently abandoned (Livarda, 2011), or failed to diffuse beyond elite gardens until much later (Langgut, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites sources documenting abandonment and limited diffusion of some crops.

claim: Limited adoption in local agriculture is a feature of some proposed IGR crops.
source: Limited adoption in local agriculture is also a feature of some proposed IGR crops, as Watson admitted regarding coconut and mango (Watson, 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites Watson's acknowledgment of limited adoption.

claim: The balance between IGR and RAD crops in the Eastern Mediterranean is about even and perhaps weighted toward RAD.
source: Thus, a cursory consideration of proposed IGR and RAD crops in the Eastern Mediterranean reveals that the balance between the two is about even and perhaps weighted toward RAD (Tables 1–2).
evidence: The manuscript compares the two sets of crops based on the tables presented.

claim: Systematic evaluation of Islamic and Roman contributions to agricultural dispersal has been attempted for Iberia.
source: Systematic evaluation of respective Islamic and Roman contributions to agricultural dispersal has been attempted for Iberia (Butzer et al., 1985; Peña-Chocarro et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies that evaluated crop dispersal in Iberia.

claim: Archaeobotanical studies in Egypt, northern Syria, and Jerusalem have yielded evidence for IGR introductions framed against Roman agricultural diffusion.
source: In the Eastern Mediterranean, archaeobotanical studies in Egypt (Van der Veen et al., 2018), northern Syria (Samuel, 2001), and Jerusalem (Amichay et al., 2019; Fuks et al., 2020a) have also yielded evidence for IGR introductions framed against Roman agricultural diffusion, but these have not yet been considered holistically.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple regional studies on crop introductions.

claim: The Negev Highlands offer an ideal test case for the geographical extent of crop dispersal as a desert region on the margins of the settled zone.
source: The Negev Highlands offer an ideal test case for the geographical extent of crop dispersal, as a desert region on the margins of the settled zone, which practiced vibrant runoff farming and engaged in Mediterranean–Red Sea trade (Kedar, 1957; Evenari et al., 1982; Tepper et al., 2020b; Bruins et al., 2019; Fuks et al., 2021a).
evidence: The manuscript argues for the suitability of the Negev Highlands as a study site and cites supporting sources.

claim: Jujube and white lupine are unprecedented in Levantine archaeobotany.
source: Several other identified economic plants, including two unprecedented in Levantine archaeobotany—jujube (Ziziphus jujuba/mauritiana) and white lupine (Lupinus albus)—implicate RAD as the greater force for crop migrations.
evidence: The manuscript states that these species have not been previously found in Levantine archaeobotany.

claim: Some of the earliest aubergine seeds in the Levant were found in the Negev Highland middens.
source: Among the findings, some of the earliest aubergine (Solanum melongena) seeds in the Levant represent the proposed IGR.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the aubergine seeds as among the earliest in the region.

claim: Crop diversity is key to sustainable agriculture and global food security.
source: Crop diversity has long been recognized as key to sustainable agriculture and global food security, encompassing genetic resources for agricultural crop improvement geared at improving yields, pest resistance, climate change resilience, and the promotion of cultural heritage.
evidence: The manuscript states a widely recognized principle in agriculture.

claim: Current global genetic diversity of agricultural crops is a product of their dispersal from multiple regions.
source: The current global genetic diversity of agricultural crops is a product of their dispersal from multiple regions and much research has attempted to reconstruct these trajectories (Vavilov, 2009; Diamond, 2002; Zohary et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites foundational works on crop dispersal and diversity.

claim: Most studies of crop dispersal have focused on prehistoric origins and developments.
source: Yet, as is true for archaeology-based domestication research in general, most studies of crop dispersal and exchange have focused on prehistoric origins and developments (Zohary and Hopf, 1973; Smith, 1989; Denham et al., 2003; Tanno and Willcox, 2006; Weiss et al., 2006; Purugganan and Fuller, 2009; Riehl et al., 2013), to the near exclusion of more recent crop histories directly affecting today's agricultural diversity.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies to support the claim about research focus.

claim: Eleven middens from Elusa, Shivta, and Nessana were excavated at approximately 10 cm height intervals.
source: Eleven middens from the three sites, Elusa, Shivta, and Nessana, were excavated at approximately 10 cm height intervals to ensure chronological control (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the excavation methodology.

claim: A three-pronged sifting strategy was adopted to maximize retrieval of artifacts and organic remains.
source: A three-pronged sifting strategy was adopted to maximize retrieval of artifacts and organic remains, while enabling complementary resolutions of analysis: (1) Most excavated sediment was dry screened on-site through 5 mm sieves. (2) Wet screening through 1 mm mesh was performed on two buckets (~20 l) from each excavated locus-basket. (3) One additional bucket from each locus-basket was set aside for fine screening.
evidence: The manuscript describes the sampling and screening methodology.

claim: Pollen from the reservoir and the northern church at Shivta contributed additional taxa.
source: Pollen from the reservoir and the northern church at Shivta contributed additional taxa, as did wood and charcoal analyses.
evidence: The manuscript describes additional sources of plant taxa identification.

claim: Results of pollen and wood analyses were previously published by Langgut et al.
source: Results of pollen and wood analyses were previously published by Langgut et al. (Langgut et al., 2021; Bar-Oz et al., 2019) and are summarized in Supplementary files 3–5.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications for pollen and wood data.

claim: The excavations' stratigraphic, ceramic, and radiocarbon analyses enabled differentiation of five chronological phases.
source: The excavations' stratigraphic, ceramic, and radiocarbon analyses enabled the differentiation of five chronological phases obtained from the middens (Bar-Oz et al., 2019; Fuks et al., 2020b): Roman (ca. 0–300 CE), Early Byzantine (ca. 300–450 CE), Middle Byzantine (ca. 450–550 CE), Late Byzantine (ca. 550–650 CE) and Umayyad (ca. 650–750 CE), which was adjusted slightly based on radiocarbon dates presented herein.
evidence: The manuscript describes the chronological framework based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Additional radiocarbon dates were obtained for loci-baskets containing unprecedented finds for Southern Levantine archaeobotany.
source: Additional radiocarbon dates were attained for loci-baskets containing unprecedented finds for Southern Levantine archaeobotany, as well as the locus-basket containing well-preserved aubergine seeds in Shivta.
evidence: The manuscript describes the radiocarbon dating strategy for key finds.

claim: Barley grains from the same sediment samples as aubergine, lupine, and jujube seeds were selected for radiocarbon dating.
source: The aubergine, lupine, and jujube seeds were too rare to sacrifice for direct radiocarbon dating so barley grains were selected from the very same sediment sample within each locus-basket and dated at the Poznan Radiocarbon Laboratory (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript explains the radiocarbon dating methodology for rare specimens.

claim: All identifications of carpological remains were made with reference to the Israel National Collection of Plant Seeds and Fruits at Bar-Ilan University.
source: All identifications of carpological remains were made with reference to the Israel National Collection of Plant Seeds and Fruits at Bar-Ilan University.
evidence: The manuscript describes the reference collection used for identifications.

claim: Cereal grain morphometry was employed to identify candidates using the Computerized Key of Grass Grains.
source: Cereal grain morphometry was employed to identify candidates, using the Computerized Key of Grass Grains developed by Mordechai Kislev's laboratory (Kislev et al., 1995; Kislev et al., 1997; Kislev et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology for cereal identification and cites the tool used.

claim: S. melongena seeds are distinguished from wild Solanum seeds by their larger size, reticulated seed coat pattern, and wide ovoid hilum.
source: S. melongena seeds are distinguished from wild Solanum seeds of the Southern Levant by their larger size, reticulated seed coat pattern, and the wide ovoid hilum set in a recess in the seed's lateral outline (Van der Veen and Morales, 2011; Amichay and Weiss, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes identification criteria and cites supporting sources.

claim: Three definitive S. melongena seeds were identified from Umayyad Shivta.
source: Based on these criteria, we identified three definitive S. melongena seeds from Umayyad Shivta (Area E, Locus 504, Basket 5029).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of aubergine seeds from a specific context.

claim: A single charred Prunus subgen. Cerasus/Prunus endocarp was found in a course-sift sample from Umayyad Shivta.
source: A single charred ovoid endocarp with a pointed apex, elliptical base (5 mm by 2.5 mm), and smooth surface was found in a course-sift sample from Umayyad Shivta (Area K1, Locus 165, Basket 1652; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the find and provides measurements.

claim: The characteristics of the endocarp ruled out apricot, peach, and almond, leaving cherry and plum as candidates.
source: The above characteristics ruled out apricot, peach, and almond, and leave cherry and plum as candidates (Prunus subgen. Cerasus/Prunus).
evidence: The manuscript describes the identification process based on morphological characteristics.

claim: Charred V. nilotica seeds were identified in midden samples from Elusa.
source: Charred V. nilotica seeds were identified using a combination of criteria (1)-(4) above in midden samples from Elusa (Area A1, Locus 1/10a; A4, L. 4/06 a-4/07 a; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of Nile acacia seeds from specific contexts.

claim: Previous archaeobotanical finds of Nile acacia in the Levant all come from Roman-period sites in the Dead Sea rift valley.
source: Previous archaeobotanical finds of Nile acacia in the Levant all come from Roman-period sites in the Dead Sea rift valley, which Kislev, 1990 interpreted as a component of the ancient flora in this area marked by pockets of Sudanian vegetation.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous finds and their interpretation.

claim: Nile acacia seed finds from Elusa are the first of their kind from outside the phytogeographic region of Sudanian vegetation.
source: Nile acacia seed finds from Elusa (Figure 3) are the first of their kind from outside the phytogeographic region of Sudanian vegetation, but they remain within the ancient caravan trade routes connecting the Red Sea and the Mediterranean.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the novelty of the Elusa finds in their geographic context.

claim: Three candidates for lupine seeds were identified among course-sifted charred archaeobotanical remains from Nessana.
source: Three candidates for lupine seeds were identified among course-sifted charred archaeobotanical remains from Nessana (Area A, Locus 101, Baskets 1008/1 and 1040/2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of lupine seeds from specific contexts.

claim: The seed coat of cultivated L. albus is much thinner than its local wild relatives.
source: As is common among domesticated legumes in general, the seed coat of cultivated L. albus is much thinner than its local wild relatives.
evidence: The manuscript describes a distinguishing characteristic of domesticated lupine.

claim: A single charred obconical-mucronate endocarp was found from Umayyad-period layers at Shivta.
source: A single charred obconical-mucronate endocarp was found from Umayyad-period layers at Shivta (Area E, Locus 501, Basket 5108).
evidence: The manuscript reports the find of a jujube endocarp from a specific context.

claim: Micro-CT scanning demonstrated the specimen to be spherically hollow with remnants of a partition, confirming its status as a fruit endocarp.
source: Micro-CT scanning was conducted using a Bruker desktop SkyScan 1174 at the Laboratory of Bone Biomechanics, Hebrew University of Jerusalem (optical resolution: 9.6 µm; exposure: 4500ms; rotation step: 0.400 degrees; 180-degree rotation option was used; 0.25 mm thick aluminum filter). The scans demonstrated the specimen to be spherically hollow with remnants of a partition (Videos 1–2), confirming its status as a fruit endocarp.
evidence: The manuscript describes the micro-CT analysis and its results.

claim: The external endocarp dimensions and obconical shape with markedly narrowing apex are unique to certain varieties of Ziziphus jujuba/mauritiana.
source: The external endocarp dimensions (11.16 mm × 6.0 mm × 5.33 mm) and its obconical with markedly narrowing apex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) are unique to certain varieties of Ziziphus jujuba/mauritiana.
evidence: The manuscript describes the morphological characteristics used for identification.

claim: Charred L. clymenum seeds were identified at Nessana and Shivta.
source: Charred L. clymenum seeds were identified at Nessana, Area A (Locus 106, Basket 1255 cf. L. 106, B. 1257; L. 101, B. 1032) and several from Area K at Shivta (L. 153, B. 1588,1610; L. 158, B. 1618; L. 166, B. 1658; L. 169, B. 1678,1703; L. 172, B. 1689).
evidence: The manuscript reports the identification of Spanish vetchling seeds from specific contexts.

claim: Identification of Lathyrus clymenum was based on morphological similarity to ancient L. clymenum seeds identified from Tel Nami.
source: Identification of Lathyrus clymenum L. was based on morphological similarity to ancient L. clymenum seeds identified from Tel Nami by Kislev et al., 1993.
evidence: The manuscript cites a comparative reference for identification.

claim: Palynological and anthracological analyses support local cultivation of grapevine, fig, olive, date, pomegranate, carob, and the Prunus genus.
source: Complementing the seed/fruit remains presented above, palynological and anthracological analyses support local cultivation of grapevine, fig, olive, date, pomegranate, carob, and the Prunus genus, which includes almond, peach, and/or plum/cherry (Langgut et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites pollen and charcoal analyses supporting local cultivation.

claim: It is plausible that stone pine was cultivated locally, albeit on a small scale.
source: Based on stone pine seed coats (Figure 3d), and the identification of Pinaceae pollen indicative of a pine other than the local Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis Mill.), it is plausible that stone pine was cultivated locally, albeit on a small scale (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript infers local cultivation based on seed and pollen evidence.

claim: Pollen evidence suggests small-scale local cultivation of hazel.
source: Pollen evidence also suggests small-scale local cultivation of hazel—an additional domesticate unattested in the Southern Levant before the Roman period (Supplementary files 4 and 5).
evidence: The manuscript infers local cultivation based on pollen evidence.

claim: Doum palm and sycomore fig are excluded from the discussion of domesticated food plants.
source: Therefore, we exclude doum palm and sycomore fig from the discussion of domesticated food plants' status and longer-term trajectories, but include them among the fruit trees in Supplementary file 5.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for excluding certain species from analysis.

claim: Sycomore fig was grown primarily for wood in ancient times.
source: Similarly, sycomore fig (Ficus sycomorus L.), which produces tasty fruits, was grown primarily for wood in ancient times (Feliks, 1968).
evidence: The manuscript cites a source on the primary use of sycomore fig.

claim: Exotic trees commonly used for quality wood and craft include cedar of Lebanon, European ash, and boxwood.
source: Other exotic trees commonly used for quality wood and craft were identified by pollen and/or charcoal, including: cedar of Lebanon (Cedrus libani A.Rich.), European ash (Fraxinus excelsior L.), and boxwood (Buxus sempervirens L.).
evidence: The manuscript identifies exotic trees based on pollen and charcoal evidence.

claim: Cedar was identified by both charcoal and pollen, suggesting local garden cultivation.
source: Cedar was identified by both charcoal and pollen, suggesting local garden cultivation (see Langgut et al., 2021 and Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript infers local cultivation based on multiple lines of evidence and cites a source.

claim: The near absence of RAD crops in the Byzantine middens compared with the Early Islamic middens is likely due to conditions favoring deposition and preservation in the latter.
source: The near absence of these crop species in the Negev Highland Byzantine middens compared with the Early Islamic middens is likely the result of conditions favoring deposition and preservation of archaeobotanical remains in the latter, such as a much higher concentration of apparently hearth-derived domestic waste.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the differential preservation patterns.

claim: The paucity of RAD crops in the Byzantine middens is not considered evidence of their absence.
source: Therefore, we do not consider the paucity of RAD crops in the Byzantine middens to be evidence of their absence.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the absence of evidence in light of preservation biases.

claim: There is no pre-Islamic evidence for aubergine in the Southern Levant.
source: However, one crop for which there is no pre-Islamic evidence in the Southern Levant is the aubergine.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of earlier evidence for aubergine.

claim: All other RAD species found in the Negev Highlands are attested to in the Southern Levantine archaeobotanical record of the 1st c. BCE–4th c. CE.
source: All other RAD species found in the Negev Highlands are attested to in the Southern Levantine archaeobotanical record of the 1st c. BCE–4th c. CE (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the temporal distribution of RAD species in the archaeobotanical record.

claim: Historical studies have identified white lupine and jujube in Roman-period texts of the Southern Levant.
source: However, historical studies have identified these species in Roman-period texts of the Southern Levant (Amar, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites a historical study documenting textual references to these species.

claim: Samples containing white lupine and jujube were dated to the Umayyad or early Abbasid period (mid-7th – late 8th c. cal. CE at 2σ).
source: Samples containing the unique finds of white lupine and non-indigenous jujube—which are unprecedented in Southern Levantine archaeobotany—were dated to the Umayyad or early Abbasid period (mid-7th – late 8th c. cal. CE at 2σ; see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript provides radiocarbon dating results for the samples.

claim: The Early Islamic introduction of aubergine is consistent with Watson's claim that summer cultivation expanded in this period.
source: In other regions of the Southern Levant, summer crops were certainly cultivated in the Roman period (Decker, 2009b; Feliks, 2008), but the Early Islamic introduction of aubergine is consistent with Watson's claim that summer cultivation expanded in this later period (Watson, 1983; Samuel, 2001; Van der Veen and Morales, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the aubergine find in relation to Watson's thesis and cites supporting sources.

claim: Widespread adoption of summer-winter crop rotation in the Mediterranean region effected changes in people's diets and work routines.
source: Ultimately, widespread adoption of summer-winter crop rotation in the Mediterranean region effected changes in people's diets and work routines.
evidence: The manuscript makes a general claim about the impact of crop rotation.

claim: These changes in diet and work routines did not occur rapidly.
source: Yet these changes clearly did not occur rapidly.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the evidence as indicating gradual change.

claim: The Early Islamic assemblages from the Negev Highlands span only the first 200–300 years of Islam.
source: To be fair, the Early Islamic assemblages from the Negev Highlands do not offer enough of a time perspective to fully gauge the effects of Early Islamic crop introduction on their own as they span only the first 200–300 years of Islam.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation in the temporal scope of the data.

claim: Finds from the 7th–8th century middens may reflect carryovers from Byzantine agronomic traditions and techniques.
source: Yet it is also possible that finds from the 7th–8th century middens reflect carryovers from Byzantine agronomic traditions and techniques.
evidence: The manuscript suggests an alternative interpretation of the Early Islamic finds.

claim: If crop introductions had been inundating and pervasive during the Early Islamic period, they would have been more apparent in Negev Highland crop diversity.
source: Had crop introductions been inundating and pervasive during the Early Islamic period, we expect they would have been more apparent in Negev Highland crop diversity.
evidence: The manuscript makes a counterfactual argument based on the observed data.

claim: The evidence supports a gradualist model for Holocene-wide crop diffusion.
source: Altogether the evidence supports a gradualist model for Holocene-wide crop diffusion, within which the first millennium CE contributed more to global agricultural diversity than any earlier period.
evidence: The manuscript draws a broad conclusion from the data about the pattern of crop diffusion.

claim: The multi-regional evidence suggests that the multi-empire combination of Roman-Byzantine and Umayyad-Abassid regimes was a major force for crop diffusion.
source: The multi-regional evidence suggests that the multi-empire combination of Roman-Byzantine and Umayyad-Abassid regimes was a major force for crop diffusion, while a likely role for developments in the Sassanid empire is underrepresented in current research.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes evidence from multiple regions to draw a conclusion about the forces driving crop diffusion.

claim: A likely role for developments in the Sassanid empire is underrepresented in current research.
source: The multi-regional evidence suggests that the multi-empire combination of Roman-Byzantine and Umayyad-Abassid regimes was a major force for crop diffusion, while a likely role for developments in the Sassanid empire is underrepresented in current research.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in current research.

claim: The combined forces underlying first millennium CE crop diffusion affected, but did not immediately transform, people's diets.
source: Yet the evidence presented here demonstrates that even the combined forces underlying first millennium CE crop diffusion affected, but did not immediately transform, people's diets.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the data to show gradual rather than rapid dietary change.

claim: The situation of reliance on Neolithic founder crops widely persisted until the latter second millennium CE.
source: Indeed, this situation widely persisted until the latter second millennium CE.
evidence: The manuscript makes a broad historical claim about dietary continuity.

claim: The first millennium CE was unprecedented for plant migrations and food diversity.
source: In conclusion, the new microregional data presented above supports an emerging multi-regional picture of both an unprecedented period for plant migrations and food diversity in the first millennium CE as well as gradual and incomplete local adoption.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding about the significance of the first millennium CE.

claim: Local adoption of first millennium CE crop introductions was gradual and incomplete.
source: In conclusion, the new microregional data presented above supports an emerging multi-regional picture of both an unprecedented period for plant migrations and food diversity in the first millennium CE as well as gradual and incomplete local adoption.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the pattern of adoption observed in the data.

claim: The first millennium CE is consistent with a long-term pattern of gradual local adoption of crops.
source: These findings present a window onto a wider perspective on the last 10+ millennia of Southwest Asian crop diffusion, in which the first millennium CE is unprecedented for the diversity of plant species in motion yet consistent with a long-term pattern of gradual local adoption.
evidence: The manuscript places the findings in a broader temporal context.
